output.rationale: This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 (along with PM10) exposure and respiratory hospital admissions using distributed lag non-linear models, which is a time-series approach. The study reports quantitative associations and risk estimates for respiratory diseases including asthma and COPD. While the focus is on comparing pre- and post-COVID periods, it meets all inclusion criteria: original research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, and reports effect estimates with statistical significance.

The study meets most inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory ED visits (asthma exacerbations) using what appears to be a time-series design (mixed-effects quasi-Poisson regression with daily data). However, the abstract does not explicitly report a relative risk, odds ratio, or equivalent effect measure with confidence interval. It only mentions statistical significance (P<10-4) and describes a non-linear sigmoid relationship. Without confirmation that quantitative effect estimates with CIs are reported in the full text, the decision remains uncertain.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) includes PM2.5 as exposure, (3) outcome is asthma hospitalization which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) uses case-crossover design (time-stratified), (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs (0.31% increase per 1-μg/m3 PM2.5, 95% CI 0.24-0.37%), and (6) published in English. Although it examines multiple pollutants, PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed and reported.

This is an original case-crossover study examining the association between PM2.5 (as the primary component of AQI) and respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits for childhood asthma. The study reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Although the primary exposure is AQI, the abstract explicitly states that PM2.5 was the primary pollutant responsible for the AQI (62% of days) and that the association was strongest for PM2.5-specific AQI. The outcome is asthma exacerbations resulting in ED visits and hospitalizations, which meets the respiratory hospitalization/ED visit criterion.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-stratified case-crossover design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcomes include respiratory hospitalizations (32 respiratory discharge diagnoses), (4) the study design is case-crossover, (5) the abstract indicates associations were estimated (effect measures) for PM2.5 and respiratory outcomes with positive associations reported for 31 of 32 respiratory outcomes, and (6) the publication appears to be in English. Although the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly includes respiratory hospitalizations as a major outcome category.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series analysis with DLNM; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) the outcome is hospital admissions for respiratory disease; (4) the study design is time-series; (5) it reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., RR=1.030, 95% CI: 1.012-1.049 for PM2.5); and (6) the article is published in English. Although multiple air pollutants are examined, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported with quantitative effect estimates.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) outcome includes both respiratory ED presentations and hospitalizations for bronchiolitis, (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with quantitative effect estimates (>10% increased risk for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. While multiple pollutants are examined (NO2, PM10, PM2.5), PM2.5 is specifically included and analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is one of the exposures examined, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (acute upper respiratory infections), (4) time-series design explicitly stated, (5) reports relative risk with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 (RR=1.0247, 95% CI: 1.0092-1.0405), and (6) published in English. Although it examines multiple pollutants, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcomes include respiratory hospitalizations and emergency department visits, (4) study design is case-crossover as explicitly stated, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. While the population is specific (childhood cancer survivors), this does not violate any exclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure (along with PM10 and NO2), reports respiratory hospitalizations (bronchiolitis) as the outcome, and provides odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. The study is published in English and reports quantitative effect estimates for PM2.5.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, (2) exposure includes fine particulate matter (PM2.5), (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations in children, (4) study design is case-crossover, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., OR=1.004 [0.955-1.056] overall and stratified estimates), and (6) appears to be published in English. Although the study also examines oxidant gases and particle constituents as effect modifiers, PM2.5 is clearly one of the primary exposures analyzed.

While this study meets several inclusion criteria (time-series design, PM2.5 exposure, reports RR with effect estimates, original research), the outcome is hospitalization specifically for SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19 infection rather than general respiratory hospitalizations. COVID-19 hospitalizations represent a specific infectious disease outcome that differs from the broader category of respiratory hospitalizations typically examined in PM2.5 systematic reviews. The review appears to focus on general respiratory hospitalizations, not disease-specific infectious outcomes.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as an exposure, (3) outcome is asthma emergency department visits (respiratory ED visits), (4) time-series study design clearly stated, (5) reports rate ratios with 95% credible intervals (e.g., RR=1.016, 95% CI: 1.008-1.025 for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Asthma ED visits are a specific type of respiratory emergency department visit, which falls within the scope of respiratory hospitalization/ED visit outcomes.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcomes include both respiratory ED presentations and hospital admissions, (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports incidence rate ratios with 95% CIs (e.g., IRR 1.043, 95% CI: 1.000-1.089 for ED presentations), and (6) published in English. No exclusion criteria apply.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) the outcome is respiratory disease hospitalizations, (4) it uses a time-series study design with generalized additive models and distributed lag nonlinear models, (5) it reports quantitative effect estimates including relative risk and percentage increases in hospitalization risk (e.g., 8.3% and 12.1% for temperature extremes, and mentions positive lag effects for PM2.5), and (6) the abstract is in English. While the study examines multiple pollutants and temperature, PM2.5 is specifically included and analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly studied as an exposure, (3) the outcome is respiratory disease hospitalizations, (4) time-series analysis with GAM was used, (5) the results indicate that effect estimates were calculated (PM2.5 and PM10 were 'associated with increased risks'), and (6) the article is in English. While the abstract does not explicitly state the numerical effect estimates with confidence intervals, it clearly indicates they were calculated and reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5 (wildfire smoke PM2.5), (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (acute respiratory infections, pneumonia, COPD, asthma, and other respiratory diseases), (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports relative risk with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly includes respiratory hospitalizations as a primary outcome.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using generalized additive Poisson model, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (hospital admissions for URTI), (4) time-series design analyzing daily data, (5) reports quantitative effect estimate with 95% CI (0.84% increase per 10 μg/m³, 95% CI 0.05-1.64%), and (6) published in English. Upper respiratory tract infections are respiratory conditions requiring hospitalization.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations for asthma and COPD. It reports quantitative risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 exposure. Although the main finding was for NO2, the study explicitly analyzed PM2.5 as one of multiple exposures and reported effect estimates with confidence intervals (RR for asthma: 0.981-1.148; RR for COPD: 0.966-1.019). This meets all inclusion criteria.

While this study meets most inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, quantitative effect estimates with CI, English language), it fails the study design criterion. This is described as a 'retrospective cohort study' rather than a time-series or case-crossover design. Although distributed lag models are used (which are common in time-series studies), the fundamental design is cohort-based with person-months of follow-up, not the required time-series or case-crossover approach.

While this is an original epidemiological study with PM2.5 exposure (from wildfire smoke), time-series design, and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the primary outcomes are cardiovascular and cerebrovascular ED visits, not respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits. Although respiratory conditions are mentioned as a secondary finding, the study's focus and design are centered on cardiovascular/cerebrovascular outcomes, making it inappropriate for a systematic review specifically on PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory ED visits (pneumonia, COPD/asthma). It uses a time-series design with distributed lag models and quasi-Poisson regression. The study reports quantitative effect estimates (RR with 95% CI) for respiratory outcomes including pneumonia. Although it also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it meets all inclusion criteria for the respiratory component.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and respiratory (pneumonia) hospitalizations with quantitative effect estimates, it uses a prospective cohort design rather than the required time-series or case-crossover design. The inclusion criteria specifically limit eligible study designs to time-series or case-crossover studies only.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory emergency room visits using a generalized additive model (consistent with time-series design). The study reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., RR = 1.011, 95%CI: 1.002, 1.020). While the study focuses on source-specific PM2.5, it also reports overall PM2.5 effects, making it eligible for inclusion.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as an exposure among multiple pollutants, (3) outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, (4) case-crossover design is clearly stated, (5) reports percentage change in odds with 95% CI (equivalent to OR), and (6) published in English. The study reports a 1.2% increase in odds of admission per 10 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5 with confidence intervals.

Although this is an original time-series study with PM2.5 exposure and quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals, the outcome is hospitalization for rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD), which is a specific autoimmune/rheumatologic condition with lung involvement, not general respiratory hospitalization. The review targets respiratory hospitalizations (e.g., asthma, COPD, pneumonia, general respiratory conditions), not hospitalizations for autoimmune diseases that happen to affect the lungs.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory ED visits as outcomes (asthma/wheeze, bronchitis, pneumonia, upper respiratory infections), provides odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and is published in English in a peer-reviewed journal.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 exposure explicitly stated, (3) respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits for asthma and COPD, (4) time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports excess rates with 95% CI (e.g., ER = 2.1%, 95% CI = 0.7%, 3.6%), and (6) appears to be in English. No exclusion criteria apply.

While the title mentions 'hospitalization', the abstract clearly describes the outcome as 'outpatient visits' for upper respiratory tract infections, not hospitalizations or ED visits. The study uses a generalized additive model (time-series design) and examines PM2.5 exposure, but does not meet the outcome criteria of respiratory hospitalization or emergency department visit.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using Poisson regression; (2) Exposure is PM2.5; (3) Outcomes include both respiratory ED visits and hospitalizations; (4) Study design is time-series (daily counts linked with daily PM2.5 estimates); (5) Reports multiple RR estimates with 95% CIs for respiratory outcomes (e.g., RR=1.25 [1.21, 1.30] for respiratory disease EDVs); (6) Published in English. The study examines both ED visits and hospitalizations for respiratory conditions, making it highly relevant to the systematic review.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations for AECOPD. The study reports quantitative effect estimates (RR with 95% CI) for the association between PM2.5 and hospitalizations. Although the study focuses on interaction effects with temperature and includes multiple pollutants, PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures. AECOPD hospitalizations are a specific type of respiratory hospitalization, meeting the outcome criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, (4) study design is time-series regression, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CI (1.61% increase per 10 μg/m3, 95% CI = 0.87, 2.35%), and (6) published in English. The use of predicted rather than measured PM2.5 does not disqualify the study as it still examines the PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization association.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) exposure is source-specific PM2.5, (3) outcomes include respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits for influenza and pneumonia, (4) case-crossover design is specified, (5) reports excess rates with 95% CIs (e.g., ER=9.2%, 95% CI: 4.3%, 14.3%), and (6) published in English. While the study examines source-specific PM2.5 rather than total PM2.5, PM2.5 is the primary exposure being analyzed.

This is an original time-series study using generalized additive models examining the association between PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and emergency department visits for upper respiratory tract infection. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 (5.302% increase, 95% CI: 3.202, 7.445 per 10 ug/m3). URTI is a respiratory condition requiring ED visits, meeting the outcome criteria. All inclusion criteria are satisfied.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a generalized additive model, which is characteristic of time-series analysis; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalization (pneumonia and asthma) in children; (4) the study design is time-series based on the methodology described (GAM with lag structure analyzing daily hospitalization rates against air pollutant concentrations); (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported (2.22% increase per 10-unit PM2.5 increase, 95%CI: 0.64%, 3.82%); and (6) the article is published in English. While multiple pollutants are analyzed, PM2.5 is specifically included and reported separately.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is asthma emergency room admissions which qualifies as respiratory ED visits, (4) time-series study design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimate with 95% CI (7.2% increase, 95% CI 1.7-13.1%), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study with case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly listed as one of the exposures assessed, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (ILD admissions are respiratory hospitalizations), (4) case-crossover design is specified, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are reported for multiple pollutants including the PM2.5 exposure of interest, and (6) published in English. While the abstract emphasizes SO2 and NO2 results, PM2.5 was measured and analyzed as stated in the methods.

While this is a time-series study that includes PM2.5 as an exposure and respiratory hospitalizations as an outcome with effect estimates reported, the abstract does not present any quantitative results (RR or CI) specifically for PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations. The results section only reports associations for NO2, ozone, and noise with various outcomes, but PM2.5 results are not mentioned despite being listed as a measured exposure. Without the PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization effect estimate, this study cannot contribute to the systematic review's objectives.

This is an original epidemiological study using time-series design (generalized additive model with distributed lag models) examining PM2.5 exposure and COPD hospitalizations. The study reports quantitative effect estimates (percent increases in daily admissions). COPD hospitalizations are a respiratory hospitalization outcome. The study meets all inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalizations, (4) it uses a case-crossover design, (5) it reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (1.73% increase, 95% CI: 1.34%, 2.12% for PM2.5), and (6) it is published in English. Although it also examines PM2.5-10, PM2.5 is explicitly included as a separate exposure.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original ecological time-series study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations (pneumonia, acute bronchitis, bronchiolitis, asthma), (4) study design is time-series, (5) reports relative risk estimates with values (RR = 1.017, 1.022, 1.020 at different lags), and (6) published in English. All key elements required for inclusion are clearly present.

The study meets most inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospital admissions with quantitative effect estimates (RR with 95% CI). However, the study design is a difference-in-differences approach with distributed lag non-linear models, which is not a standard time-series or case-crossover design as specified in the inclusion criteria. While it uses time-series data (daily PM2.5 and admissions), the analytical approach differs from conventional time-series methods. This warrants expert judgment on whether this methodological variation should be included in the systematic review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome is emergency department visits for respiratory diseases (COPD and upper respiratory diseases), (4) uses a case-crossover study design, (5) reports positive associations (effect estimates) for PM2.5 with various lag periods, and (6) published in English. While the abstract does not explicitly state the type of effect measure (OR/RR), case-crossover studies typically report odds ratios, and the mention of 'positive results' indicates quantitative associations were calculated.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization for acute lower respiratory infections including pneumonia, COPD exacerbations, and bronchitis, (4) study design is explicitly stated as time-series, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates as percent increases with 95% confidence intervals for a 10-μg/m3 increase in PM2.5, and (6) published in English. No exclusion criteria apply.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure and hospital admissions across multiple disease categories, including respiratory diseases. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals (e.g., percentage increases in hospital admissions per 10-μg/m3 increase in PM2.5). Although the study examines multiple outcomes beyond respiratory hospitalizations, respiratory diseases are explicitly included as one of the major disease categories analyzed, making it eligible for inclusion in the systematic review.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure and asthma emergency room visits. It uses generalized additive model with Poisson regression on daily counts of ERVs, reports relative risks with 95% CIs for PM2.5 effects on respiratory (asthma) emergency department visits. Although the study also examines PM2.5-bound PAHs, it explicitly reports PM2.5 effects separately and meets all inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly studied as an exposure, (3) the outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, (4) it uses a time-series design with generalized additive models, (5) it reports percentage change with 95% CI (equivalent to effect estimates), and (6) the abstract is in English. The study provides quantitative effect estimates for PM2.5 (0.755%; 95% CI: 0.422, 1.089% per 10 μg/m3 increase).

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as an exposure with quantitative results reported, (3) outcome is asthma-related emergency department visits (AEDv), which qualifies as respiratory ED visits, (4) time-series study design explicitly stated, (5) relative risks with specific effect estimates are reported (4.4% increase per IQR increase in PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants are analyzed, PM2.5 is one of them with separate effect estimates provided.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma-related hospital admissions and emergency department visits (respiratory hospitalizations), (4) case-crossover study design is clearly stated, (5) the abstract mentions positive associations and 95% confidence intervals indicating effect estimates were reported, and (6) published in English. While the study examines multiple pollutants and effect modification, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed as an exposure of interest.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations using a time-series design (GAM). The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs for the association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospital admissions (1.03% increase per 10 μg/m3, 95% CI: 0.50%-1.56%). Although the study examines multiple outcomes beyond respiratory hospitalizations, it meets all inclusion criteria for the systematic review.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other particle metrics) and hospital admissions including respiratory outcomes. While the abstract emphasizes cardiovascular results, it explicitly states that secondary pollutants including PM2.5 were important for respiratory outcomes. The study uses Poisson regression time-series analysis and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals. It examines emergency hospital admissions which meets the outcome criteria.

This is an original time-series study using GAMs that examines PM2.5 exposure and multiple health outcomes including respiratory hospitalizations. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs for respiratory system diseases (NO2: 1.36%, 95%CI: 0.74-1.98%). Although the study examines multiple pollutants and multiple disease categories, it meets all inclusion criteria: it includes PM2.5 as an exposure, respiratory hospitalizations as one of the outcomes, uses a time-series design, and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure includes PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization and ED visits for asthma exacerbations, (4) time-series study design using Poisson regression, (5) reports RR with 95% CI for PM2.5 exposure, and (6) published in English. Asthma exacerbations requiring hospitalization/ED visit are a specific type of respiratory hospitalization.

Although this is a time-series study examining respiratory ED visits with effect estimates reported, and PM2.5 was included as a covariate in the model, the primary exposure of interest is thunderstorm-related climate parameters (precipitation and temperature), not PM2.5. The results explicitly state that PM2.5 levels were not significantly associated with asthma ED visits on thunderstorm days, indicating PM2.5 was controlled for as a confounder rather than being the exposure of interest. The study does not report effect estimates for PM2.5 association with respiratory outcomes as the main finding.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design with generalized additive model; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalizations (acute lower respiratory tract infections including pneumonia and bronchitis); (4) the study design is time-series; (5) relative risks with 95% confidence intervals are reported for PM2.5 (RR=1.0064, 95% CI 1.0004-1.0124 for pneumonia at lag4 and RR=1.0133, 95% CI 1.0025-1.0242 for bronchitis at lag010); and (6) the abstract is in English. While the study examines multiple pollutants, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported separately.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure (along with PM10), reports respiratory hospitalizations for asthma and COPD as outcomes, provides odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and appears to be published in English.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 (along with UFP) exposure and respiratory hospital admissions using a time-series design with Poisson regression. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for the association between PM2.5 and respiratory admissions (7.5% increase, 95% CI: 4.9-10.2% per 12.4 μg/m3 increase). All inclusion criteria are met.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, (4) time-series study design using Poisson regression, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates (percentage increases in hospitalization rates per 10 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5 with specific values for overall and stratified analyses), and (6) published in English. No exclusion criteria apply.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations, (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CI (1.74% increase per 10-μg/m3, 95% CI: 1.41-2.07% for respiratory admissions), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (159,365 respiratory disease admissions), (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CI (1.95% increase per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5 for respiratory diseases, 95% CI 1.63-2.27%), and (6) published in English. Although it also examines cardiovascular outcomes, respiratory hospitalizations are clearly analyzed and reported.

While this is a time-series study examining respiratory hospitalizations with effect estimates, the primary exposure is particle oxidative potential (OP), not PM2.5 mass concentration itself. The study uses PM2.5 as a carrier to express OP measures (OP per m³), but the exposure of interest and the reported associations are for oxidative potential metrics (OP(AA) and OP(GSH)), not PM2.5 concentration. This does not meet the inclusion criterion requiring PM2.5 as the exposure.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) exposure and emergency department visits for pediatric asthma. The study uses a time-series design with Poisson generalized linear models and daily data from 2002-2010. It reports rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals for the association between PM2.5 sources and respiratory ED visits. All inclusion criteria are met.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using GAM for time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly studied as an exposure, (3) respiratory disease hospitalization is the outcome, (4) the study design is time-series based on the use of GAM to estimate short-term effects, (5) quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals are reported (e.g., 1.95% increase with 95% CI: 0.25, 3.67 per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5), and (6) the article is in English. Although PM10 is also analyzed, PM2.5 is included as one of the exposures.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (specifically asthma hospitalizations are reported), (4) study design is time-series, (5) reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.35 for asthma), and (6) published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly reports respiratory hospitalization outcomes which are relevant to the review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) outcome is chronic respiratory disease (CRD) hospitalizations, (4) time-series design clearly stated, (5) reports excess risks with 95% CIs for PM2.5 (2.13%, 95% CI: 0.55%, 3.74% per 10 μg/m3 increase), and (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants are examined, PM2.5 results are specifically reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory healthcare visits (which includes hospitalizations/ED visits), (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with effect estimates for PM2.5 increases, and (6) published in English. While the abstract uses the term 'healthcare visits' rather than explicitly stating 'hospitalization' or 'ED visit', respiratory healthcare encounters in this context typically refer to hospital-based care.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-stratified case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome is hospitalization for respiratory diseases, (4) the study design is case-crossover, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported (OR=1.017, 95%CI: 1.003-1.031 for PM2.5), and (6) the article appears to be published in English. The study analyzes multiple pollutants including PM2.5, which is acceptable per the inclusion criteria.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other exposures) and respiratory outcomes including ED visits and hospitalizations (inpatient visits) for asthma exacerbation. The study reports rate ratios with confidence intervals. Although the primary focus is on effect modification by viral infections and the main results presented are for pollen, the abstract indicates PM2.5 was analyzed and the study meets all inclusion criteria.

This study meets the inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a generalized additive model (GAM), which is consistent with time-series methodology; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) the outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (patients with respiratory diseases comorbid with diabetes); (4) the GAM approach with daily data indicates a time-series design; (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are reported (7.25% increase per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5); (6) the article appears to be in English. While the population is restricted to those with diabetes comorbidity, the outcome still represents respiratory hospitalizations, which meets the inclusion criteria.

While this study meets most inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, time-series design, PM2.5 exposure, reports RR with CI), the outcome is acute upper respiratory tract infections (AURTIs) which are typically minor infections like common cold, pharyngitis, etc. The systematic review focuses on respiratory hospitalizations, which generally refer to more severe lower respiratory conditions (pneumonia, COPD exacerbations, asthma) requiring hospital admission. AURTIs represent a different clinical entity and severity level than the target outcome.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using generalized additive models, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as an exposure, (3) the outcome is emergency department visits for asthma (a respiratory condition), (4) it uses a time-series study design as stated in the title and methods, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported (e.g., 6.1% increase, CI: 2.1-10.3%), and (6) the article is in English. The study examines respiratory ED visits specifically for asthma, which falls under respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations, (4) uses case time series analysis (a variant of time-series design), (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CI (1.43% increase per 10 μg/m³ increment, 95% CI: 1.34%, 1.52% for respiratory hospitalizations), and (6) published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (COPD admissions), (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimate with 95% CI (1.6%, 95% CI: 0.6%, 2.7% per 10 μg/m3 increase), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is examined as an exposure, (3) respiratory hospitalizations are included as an outcome (916,388 respiratory admissions), (4) it uses a case-crossover design as stated in the title and confirmed by the use of conditional logistic regression, (5) it reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs (0.26% increase per 10 μg/m³ PM2.5 for respiratory admissions, 95% CI = 0.22%, 0.31%), and (6) it is published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory hospitalizations (pneumonia) as the outcome, provides quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (12% and 4% increases in admissions), and appears to be published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using GAM time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome is hospital admissions for asthma, which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) the study design is time-series, (5) it reports relative risk values with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 (RR=1.015, 95% CI: 1.003-1.028 per 10 μg/m3 increase), and (6) the article appears to be published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome is hospital admissions for acute bronchitis (a respiratory hospitalization), (4) it uses a time-series study design with generalized additive models, (5) it reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (1.23% increase per 10 µg/m3 PM2.5 with 95% CI 0.21-2.26%), and (6) the abstract is in English.

While this is an original time-series study examining respiratory hospitalizations with quantitative effect estimates, the exposure is PM10, not PM2.5. While this is a time-series study examining fine particles (likely PM2.5) and asthma hospitalizations, the abstract explicitly states that 'no pollutant alone made a significant contribution to explained variance' and does not report specific effect estimates (RR, OR, or CI) for PM2.5. The study examines ozone exposure (not PM2.5) and the outcomes are cellulitis (skin infection) and pharyngitis (throat infection), not respiratory hospitalizations. The exposure is ozone, not PM2.5. While the study meets other criteria (case-crossover design, ED visits, reports OR with CI), it does not meet the fundamental inclusion criterion requiring PM2.5 as the exposure of interest.

While this study uses GAM models and evaluates air pollution health effects, it employs a before-after comparative design rather than time-series or case-crossover methodology. This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design (Quasi-Poisson generalized additive model) examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations (AECOPD admissions). This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as one of the exposures, (3) the outcome is asthma emergency department visits which qualifies as respiratory ED visits, (4) it uses a time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) the abstract mentions quantifying associations and reporting ED visit odds, indicating effect estimates are provided, and (6) the publication appears to be in English. While PM2.5 is analyzed alongside other pollutants, this is acceptable per the inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design with DLNM, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of multiple exposures, (3) outcome is COPD hospitalizations which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) time-series study design, (5) reports RR with 95% CI for PM2.5 (RR=1.048, 95%CI: 1.030-1.067), and (6) published in English. COPD hospitalizations are a specific type of respiratory hospitalization that fits the outcome criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (COPD and respiratory infection), (4) time-series study design explicitly stated, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 1.28% increase per 10-µg/m3 for heart failure), and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it clearly includes respiratory hospitalizations as specified outcomes.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5 (source-specific fine particulate matter), (3) outcome is respiratory disease emergency department visits, (4) study design is time-series (Poisson time-series regression models), (5) the abstract indicates associations were estimated (effect measures reported), and (6) published in English in Environmental Health Perspectives. While the study examines source-specific PM2.5 rather than total PM2.5, the exposure is still PM2.5 ≤2.5 µm.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as one of the exposures analyzed (PM2.5 components and criteria pollutants including PM2.5), (3) outcome includes respiratory ED visits (asthma/wheeze, bronchitis, pneumonia, URI), (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. While the study examines multiple pollutants and mixtures, PM2.5 and its components are clearly part of the analysis.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed among multiple pollutants, (3) outcome is hospital admission for bronchiectasis which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) time-series study design, (5) reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (RR=1.067, 95%CI 1.020-1.116 for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-stratified case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as an exposure, (3) the outcome is pneumonia hospitalizations which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) it reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (OR=1.015, 95% CI: 1.010-1.021 for PM2.5), and (5) appears to be published in English. The study examines both PM2.5 and PM10, but PM2.5 is one of the primary exposures analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is asthma emergency department visits (respiratory ED visits), (4) time-series study design explicitly stated, (5) reports percent increases with 95% confidence intervals for multiple age groups, and (6) published in English. Asthma ED visits are a specific type of respiratory emergency department visit.

This is an original epidemiological study examining the association between PM2.5 exposure and daily respiratory hospitalizations using time-series methods (GAM and DLNM). All inclusion criteria are met: original research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, and effect estimates with CIs reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) examines PM2.5 exposure (along with its constituents), (3) includes respiratory hospitalizations as outcomes (specifically pneumonia mentioned with ER% 1.9-5.1%), (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports excess risk percentages with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. While the study examines multiple health outcomes including cardiovascular, it explicitly reports results for respiratory causes including pneumonia.

This is an original epidemiological study examining fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure and respiratory hospitalizations in children. The study meets all inclusion criteria: original research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, and reports effect estimates with measures of association.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory emergency department visits for AECOPD patients, (4) time-series study design explicitly stated, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs (3.5% increase per 10 μg/m³ PM2.5), and (6) published in English. While this study examines respiratory hospitalizations using a case-crossover design and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the primary exposure is organic carbon (OC) species and their chemical groups (n-alkanes, hopanes, cyclohexanes, PAHs, isoalkanes), not PM2.5. Although PM2.5 is mentioned in the background as context, the actual analysis focuses on specific organic compounds as the exposure of interest. The study specifically provides effect estimates for PM2.5 exposure on respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) exposure includes PM2.5 total mass and its components, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations, (4) case-crossover design explicitly stated, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates (0.5-2.0% per IQR increase) with statistical significance noted, and (6) published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design to examine PM2.5 exposure (specifically wildfire smoke PM2.5) and respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits. The exposure is PM2.5, outcomes include both ED visits and hospitalizations for respiratory conditions, and quantitative effect estimates are provided.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using time-series analysis, examines PM2.5 exposure, includes respiratory hospitalizations as an outcome, and reports quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals (posterior intervals) for respiratory hospitalizations. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma hospital admissions (respiratory hospitalization), (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes and other PM sizes, PM2.5 and respiratory ED visits are clearly analyzed and reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory ED visits for asthma, (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CI (1.96%, 95%CI: 0.02, 3.94), and (6) published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) the outcome is respiratory disease hospitalization, (4) it uses a time-series study design with generalized additive models, (5) it reports quantitative effect estimates (percent increase per 10-μg/m³ increment) for PM2.5 and other pollutants, and (6) the abstract is in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original case-crossover epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5 from Asian Dust Storms, (3) outcome includes respiratory disease emergency room visits, (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals for respiratory diseases (OR=1.86, 95% CI: 1.30-2.91), and (6) published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original time-series epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly studied as one of the exposures, (3) respiratory emergency department visits are among the outcomes examined (asthma/wheeze and respiratory disease visits are mentioned), (4) it uses a time-series design with Poisson regression models, (5) the methods indicate associations were estimated with effect measures for interquartile range changes in pollutants, and (6) it is published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory-related hospitalizations, (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., OR per 5 µg/m3 increase in 3-day lag PM2.5: 0.971 (0.885, 1.066) for respiratory hospitalizations), and (6) published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using time-series design; (2) Exposure is PM2.5 (fine particulate matter); (3) Outcome is respiratory hospitalizations (ICD-10 codes J04.0, J12.0-J18.9, J20.0-J21.9, J45.0); (4) Time-series design explicitly stated; (5) Reports relative risk (RR=1.04) with quantitative effect estimates; (6) Published in English (with Portuguese translation). This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure includes PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory ED visits for COPD, (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CIs (6.6% increase, 95% CI 0.5-13.0% for PM2.5), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is hospital visits for pneumonia which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) uses time-series design with generalized additive Poisson regression, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates (risk ratios) with 95% confidence intervals (1.3% increase per 10-μg/m3 PM2.5), and (6) published in English. This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcomes include both respiratory hospitalizations (COPD) and ED visits (asthma), (4) quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals are reported (e.g., 0.4% (0.0%, 0.8%) for asthma ED visits in BEFORE period), and (5) appears to be published in English.
